title: Mole Cricket: How to Spot It and Stop It in Your Palay
metaTitle: Mole Cricket: Damage and Control in Rice Seedbeds
metaDescription: The mole cricket cuts seedlings at the base and leaves bare patches in the seedbed. Learn the signs and the control steps that work in rice.
excerpt: The mole cricket, Gryllotalpa orientalis, is a plump, brown, digging insect that cuts seeds, roots and seedlings from below the soil. It strikes at night, so farmers often see only the bare patches. This page shows the signs and the steps that keep it down.

heroImage.alt: A mole cricket, Gryllotalpa orientalis, brown with shovel shaped front legs for digging
heroImage.credit: Alexander A. Fomichev, CC BY, via iNaturalist

blocks.text:
The mole cricket lives in all rice environments, but it prefers upland and non flooded ground. In a flooded paddy it swims in the water or stays in permanent burrows along the levees and field borders.

Farmers care because it attacks the crop when it is smallest. It feeds on sown seeds, roots and young tillers, so a patch of seedlings can vanish and the stand loses plants. The risk is highest from seedling to tillering.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: From sowing to tillering, mostly at night, and most often in seedbeds and fields that are still dry before flooding.
Adults and nymphs live in burrows marked by soil heaps, mostly in moist, non flooded ground and along levees. Females lay shiny gray eggs in holes in the soil, and the nymphs feed on seeds and roots.

blocks.text: Look for small mounds of loose soil and burrows near the roots, and for tan nymphs in tunnels. The adult is a brownish, plump insect, about 25 to 40 millimeters long. It has short antennae and wide front legs that dig like a mole. The damage looks like ant damage. It can also resemble a [white grub](/pests/white-grub) problem, but white grubs only eat roots and do not cut the stem at the base.

items: Seedlings are cut at the base and bare patches show in the seedbed or field.
Seeds are eaten after sowing, so the stand comes up thin.
Roots are chewed, and young plants grow poorly or die.
Burrows and small heaps of soil appear near the roots and along the levees.
Damage grows at night and the insects hide in the soil by day.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Ant damage and [cutworm](/pests/cutworm) damage also cut seedlings. Look for the burrows with soil heaps and for the digging insect itself to be sure.
How Mole Cricket Hurts Your Palay

The mole cricket causes loss of plant stand, cut seedlings and root damage, as the IRRI based rice pest key describes. The damage comes in patches, not across the whole field. Even so, a thin stand costs seed, labor for replanting and time.

We found no sourced yield loss figure for the Philippines, so we give none. Check your seedbed every few days, and mark the patches in your notes so you can compare them next season.

items: Flood the field for 3 to 4 days. Standing water drives the insects out of the soil and removes the eggs. Keep water in the field where you can.
Level the field well. A level field holds water evenly and stops dry pockets where the insects stay.
Shave the bunds and plaster them with fresh wet soil. This kills the eggs laid in the levees.
Collect the nymphs and adults by hand during land preparation, and avoid raised nurseries, since dry raised beds invite damage.
Protect natural enemies. Sphecid wasps, carabid beetles, nematodes and fungi attack the mole cricket, and the crickets also eat each other.
If damage continues, use a bait on the bunds at night. Mix moistened rice bran with an insecticide and place it where the insects feed.

blocks.text: Use an insecticide only as a last resort, and only as a bait on the bunds. It corrects a problem and does not prevent one. The sources we used do not name an active ingredient. Ask your local DA office which FPA registered product to use, and follow its label.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different insecticide group next time, so the pest does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to integrated pest management](/pests/integrated-pest-management) explains how.

items: Level the field and keep water control good from the start.
Shave and plaster the bunds before every season.
Flood the field for a few days before sowing where you can.
Check the seedbed at dusk and early morning for burrows and cut seedlings.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Mole Cricket

items.q: What kind of mole cricket attacks rice?
items.a: It is the oriental mole cricket, Gryllotalpa orientalis, which lives in all rice environments.

items.q: When does the mole cricket attack rice?
items.a: From seedling to tillering. Young, newly planted seedlings are most at risk early in the season, before the field is flooded.
Standing water helps a lot. Flooding for 3 to 4 days and keeping water in the field are recommended, but the insects can still live in the levees.
Usually not. Cultural and natural control come first. A bait is the last step and must follow a registered product label.
